concepts: Integrate environmental mechanisms in climate, soil, water and ecosystems with quantitative evidence, life-cycle/circular-resource analysis, energy solutions and the economics/governance/communication of environmental responses.

Study ecosystem condition and resilience through actual biodiversity, conservation, evolutionary and biological mechanisms, coupled with soil/water science, environmental chemistry, remediation and land-use effects.

Study how institutions, markets, collective choices and behaviour shape environmental responses. Join actual policy/economic methods, qualitative/quantitative evidence and sustainability communication to a concrete environmental-science and resource/water foundation.
conceptFreeze.conceptDecision: Reconstruct the strongest integrated environmental-science response, then test ecological-resilience and environmental-policy/economic responses sequentially. Retain four evidenced candidate families and respect maximum-three stopping. Remove generic media/race, peace/conflict and trade claims; add actual LCA, environmental communication, public-policy and externality/public-goods methods where concepts support them. Source-dependent comparison approval remains conditional on the verified external thesis pathway.
conceptFreeze.schedulingRefinement: The first and policy palettes each initially had13spring-only courses. Replace closest-option hazard breadth with actual introductory economic foundations, and the policy option generic social psychology with physical renewable-energy appraisal. Both strengthen the already frozen interdisciplinary environmental concept and fit current offerings; no academic no-match or restored offerings is inferred.

courses.name: Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine
courses.rationale: Biomolecules, cells, enzymes/energy metabolism, DNA/heredity and gene expression supply concrete molecular foundations for the ecological option’s evolution, microbial/biogeochemical and biodiversity study. Biomedical examples are complementary; human disease is not presented as an Earth-system specialism.

availableEvidence.description2: Introduces biochemistry, macromolecules, cells, organ systems, DNA and cell function. Connects fundamentals to health and disease and serves as a starting point for medicine, biomedical science, life science or public health; no lab experience needed.
availableEvidence.profile: Introduces the molecular and cellular foundations of life and biomedical science. Students study biological molecules, cells and membranes, communication, enzymes and energy metabolism, cell division, DNA and heredity, gene expression, genomes and biotechnology. Scientific experiments and papers are analyzed through short teaching contributions and a research-based mini-symposium. A responsive final component selects additional life- and biomedical-science topics with the class.
availableEvidence.topics: Biological molecules and chemistry of life; Cells, organelles and membranes; Cellular communication; Enzymes and energy metabolism; Cell cycle and division; DNA and heredity; Gene mutation and molecular medicine; Gene-expression regulation and epigenetics; Genomes; Recombinant DNA and biotechnology
availableEvidence.methods: Scientific-literature searching and synthesis; Analysis of published biological experiments

courses.name: Conservation Biology
courses.rationale: Habitat loss/fragmentation, climate impacts, invasive species, conservation priorities and threatened-species assessment provide concrete ecosystem-resilience responses to environmental and land-use pressures.

availableEvidence.description2: This course explores environmental conservation through biological and social science perspectives. Topics include biodiversity importance, threats to ecosystems, conservation methods, and tools to monitor and protect nature. It also covers national and international laws, policies, and initiatives aimed at preserving ecosystems and ensuring a sustainable future for current and future generations.
availableEvidence.profile: Introduces conservation biology through biodiversity loss, its human causes and possible responses. Students examine habitat destruction and fragmentation, overharvesting, invasive species, climate change, disasters and extinction, followed by conservation planning, species management and conservation in altered landscapes. A local threatened-species project investigates conservation status and protection measures and develops a public-awareness flyer.
availableEvidence.topics: Biodiversity and ecosystems; Anthropogenic extinction; Habitat loss and fragmentation; Overharvesting; Invasive species; Climate impacts; Natural and human-caused disasters; Conservation priorities; Endangered-species management; Human-modified landscapes; People and conservation; Conservation-study design and evaluation
availableEvidence.methods: Threatened-species conservation-status analysis; Assessment of species-protection measures; Evidence-based conservation communication

courses.name: Natural Hazards, Risks & Adaptations
courses.rationale: The available description substantively supports geoscience risk analysis, climate-related/mining disasters, drought and toxic-algal hazards and adaptation. It supplies direct environmental-risk content without invented modelling software or field assessment methods.

availableEvidence.description2: Covers geoscience principles and analytical tools to understand natural disasters. Compares risks from climate change‑driven events and mining disasters and teaches actions to reduce risks from events like earthquakes, droughts and toxic algae blooms.

courses.name: Social Movements & Environmental Justice
courses.rationale: The description supports actual environmental-justice and social-movement cases, including anti-colonial/feminist/degrowth perspectives. These provide a specific societal appraisal of environmental interventions and affected communities; not a physical hazard model.

availableEvidence.description2: Focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice. Uses case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas and integrates perspectives such as feminism, anti‑colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding to encourage civic engagement.

courses.name: Building with Nature
courses.rationale: Nature-based infrastructure, coastal/river/estuary management, habitat connectivity and intervention design supply a concrete adaptation application linking physical water risks to ecosystem processes.

availableEvidence.description2: Introduces the sustainable engineering approach of working with natural processes for flood protection, land reclamation and port development. Covers history and principles of ecosystem‑based design, explores case studies and includes guest lectures and field excursions.
availableEvidence.profile: Introduces approaches that combine human infrastructure with natural processes and ecosystem health, with particular attention to Zeeland and the history of water management on Walcheren. Students examine applications across sandy and muddy coasts, lowland lakes, rivers and estuaries, cities and ports. Projects investigate ecological connectivity and formulate a Building with Nature intervention; a practical wall-building project explores constructed structures.
availableEvidence.topics: Nature-based infrastructure; Coastal and water management; Walcheren's water-management history; Sandy and muddy coasts; Lowland lakes; Rivers and estuaries; Urban nature-based solutions; Harbour habitats; Habitat connectivity; Ecoducts and fish ladders
availableEvidence.methods: Building with Nature case analysis; Ecological-corridor project analysis; Nature-based intervention design; Construction and testing of model walls

courses.name: Dynamic Earth
courses.rationale: Rocks/minerals, sedimentation/facies, structural deformation, stratigraphy and tectonic/geophysical processes directly implement geological Earth science, including field mapping, cross-sections and reconstruction of geological history.

availableEvidence.description2: Introduces Earth Science by focusing on interactions among the deep earth, lithosphere and hydrosphere. Highlights key cycles shaping Earth’s surface and includes indoor/outdoor labs and a multi‑day field excursion.
availableEvidence.profile: Introduces Earth science by linking surface geology to deep-Earth and geophysical processes. Students study rocks, minerals, sedimentation, deformation, stratigraphy, plate tectonics, seismology, the mantle and core, and interactions with climate and other Earth systems. Field and practical work teaches observation and measurement, rock and mineral identification, and reconstruction of geological history. An Ardennes field investigation produces a geological cross-section, stratigraphic column and interpretive report.
availableEvidence.topics: Plate tectonics and the Wilson cycle; Minerals and rock formation; Volcanism and metamorphism; Sedimentation and facies; Structural deformation; Stratigraphy and palaeontology; Seismology and seismic waves; Geomagnetism and gravity; Mantle and core processes; Earth-system and climate interactions; Geological history; Geohazards
availableEvidence.methods: Geological field observation and measurement; Rock and mineral identification; Geological mapping and profiling; Stratigraphic-column construction; Geological cross-section construction; Sediment and facies interpretation; Geological-history reconstruction

courses.name: The Science of Evolution
courses.rationale: Selection, genetic drift, adaptation, population genetics, phylogeny and biogeography supply specific biological mechanisms for changing communities and biodiversity. They complement ecosystem response and do not substitute for soil/water physics.

availableEvidence.description2: Evolution is the unifying theory in biology. As such, an understanding of evolutionary biology is vital for understanding the natural world. In this course, we will discuss key concepts in evolution such as population genetics, variation and selection, speciation, macro-evolution and the origins of life. The importance of evolutionary concepts to all other fields of biology will be emphasized, as well as important implications of evolutionary processes in fields like human health and climate change.
availableEvidence.profile: Examines evolutionary theory from genetic mechanisms to the diversification and history of life. Students study natural selection, variation and drift, population and quantitative genetics, adaptation and sexual reproduction, then species concepts, speciation, phylogeny and macroevolution. Genomics, development, biogeography and coevolution extend the account across scales. A project reconstructs a chosen species' evolutionary history using Tinbergen's four questions.
availableEvidence.topics: Evidence for evolution; Molecular and Mendelian genetics; Natural selection and genetic drift; Multilocus and quantitative genetics; Adaptation and units of selection; Sexual reproduction; Species concepts and speciation; Phylogeny and classification; Evolutionary biogeography; Evolutionary genomics and development; Coevolution; Evolutionary rates, extinction and radiation
availableEvidence.methods: Evolutionary-history analysis using Tinbergen's four questions; Phylogenetic reconstruction

courses.name: Marine Biology
courses.rationale: Physical/chemical oceanography, primary/secondary production, microbial and estuarine/marine ecosystems, acidification and human impacts support coastal biosphere–water interactions. Marine outreach methods do not establish hydrological instrumentation.

availableEvidence.description2: Studies ecological processes in marine environments such as estuaries, rocky shores and coral reefs. Examines human impacts and includes guest lectures, lab visits, excursions and field work, culminating in an essay.
availableEvidence.profile: Examines marine ecological processes, ocean systems and human impacts on the sea. Physical and chemical oceanography support the study of primary and secondary production, microbial ecology, and habitats from estuaries and shores to the open ocean, deep sea and polar regions. Student seminars address fisheries, aquaculture, acidification, sea-level rise and plastic pollution. A multimedia outreach project translates a marine biological topic for a public audience.
availableEvidence.topics: Physical and chemical oceanography; Primary and secondary production; Marine microbial ecology; Estuaries; Rocky and sandy shores; Pelagic and continental-shelf ecosystems; Deep-sea ecosystems; Mangroves and seagrass; Coral reefs; Polar marine environments; Fisheries and aquaculture; Ocean acidification and sea-level rise; Marine plastic pollution
availableEvidence.methods: Multimedia marine-science communication

courses.name: Earth's Resources
courses.rationale: The description supports substantial geoscientific research on nuclear-waste storage, geothermal energy and CO2 capture through literature review, reports and professional presentation. This is direct subsurface/resource inquiry, not documented lowland sedimentary logging or a required bachelor thesis.

availableEvidence.description2: Provides in‑depth geoscience research into resource and environmental challenges such as nuclear waste storage, geothermal energy and CO₂ capture. Students conduct literature reviews and produce class reports for presentation to a professional conference.

courses.name: Sustainable Farming & Innovation
courses.rationale: Environmental impacts of agriculture, biodiversity/ecosystem effects and comparative appraisal of alternative farming practices directly support land-use, soil/water and biosphere resilience. Its literature project is not a prescribed soil-physics field experiment.

availableEvidence.description2: Discusses environmental impacts of agriculture and explores sustainable agriculture approaches such as agroecology, organic farming, conservation agriculture, precision agriculture, sustainable livestock farming, agroforestry, permaculture, crop rotation, integrated pest management and sustainable supply chains.
availableEvidence.profile: Examines how food production can balance human needs with environmental impacts. Students assess current agriculture, horticulture and animal husbandry, their effects on biodiversity and ecosystems, and alternative practices and innovations. Aquaculture, alternative animal-protein sources and farming for other industries extend the comparison. A literature-based project critically investigates a chosen sustainable-farming question and reports the evidence without prescribing a single preferred approach.
availableEvidence.topics: Agricultural and horticultural systems; Environmental impacts of farming; Wildlife and biodiversity; Modification of current farming practices; Alternative agricultural approaches; Animal husbandry; Aquaculture; Alternative protein sources; Farming for non-food industries; Sustainable-farming innovation
availableEvidence.methods: Scientific-literature review; Comparative appraisal of farming practices and innovations

courses.name: Foundations of Comparative Politics
courses.rationale: Institutions, representation, interest groups, participation and policy, with actual comparative empirical inquiry, supply concrete mechanisms for comparing environmental governance settings. It is complementary political analysis, not environmental-law training.

availableEvidence.description2: Provides analytical tools to compare political systems and democracies. Examines phenomena like democratic backsliding, decline of political parties, rise of populism, media changes, non‑majoritarian institutions and globalization’s impact on domestic politics.
availableEvidence.profile: Introduces empirical comparison of political systems, with democracy, democratization and autocratization as central concerns. Students study political institutions, rules, actors and behaviour, including parties, elections, participation, polarization, interest groups and policy. Research exercises operationalize and measure democracy using V-Dem data and compare academic literature-search tools. A qualitative or quantitative research memo answers a theoretically grounded comparative-politics question through empirical analysis.
availableEvidence.topics: Democracy and authoritarianism; Democratization and democratic backsliding; States, nations and nationalism; Constitutions and courts; Executives, legislatures and bureaucracies; Political economy; Parties and party systems; Populism and technocracy; Elections and electoral systems; Political culture and polarization; Political participation; Interest groups and public policy
availableEvidence.methods: Theory-driven qualitative and quantitative research; Concept operationalization and democracy measurement; V-Dem data analysis; Comparative case analysis; Academic literature searching with OpenAlex and AI tools; Empirical election analysis; Research-question formulation

courses.name: Microeconomics & Behavior
courses.rationale: Actual uncertainty, behavioural limitations, market efficiency/failure, externalities and government intervention give substantive mechanisms for analysing environmental incentives and regulation. Applications are broader than environmental policy.

availableEvidence.description2: Study how consumers and producers make decisions under scarcity. Explore key concepts such as rational choice, decision-making under uncertainty, and non-egoistic preferences. Analyze market structures, strategic interactions, and factor markets. Learn how markets function and examine the impact of regulation. Develop analytical tools to better understand behavior and engage with empirical research.
availableEvidence.profile: Develops microeconomic theory through consumer behaviour, imperfectly competitive markets and economy-wide allocation. Students examine choice under uncertainty, non-egoistic preferences and cognitive limitations, then monopoly, strategic behaviour and labour and capital markets. General equilibrium, efficiency, externalities and government complete the analysis. Algebraic problem-solving and graphical analysis are connected to the interpretation and evaluation of research papers.
availableEvidence.topics: Choice under uncertainty; Non-egoistic preferences; Cognitive limitations; Monopoly; Imperfect competition and strategic behaviour; Labour markets; Capital markets; General equilibrium; Market efficiency; Externalities; Government intervention
availableEvidence.methods: Algebraic microeconomic analysis; Graphical economic analysis; Critical evaluation of economic research

courses.name: European Union Politics
courses.rationale: EU actors, institutions, agenda setting, legislation/implementation and actual legislative-document/process research support the regional political machinery of environmental governance. A specific environmental bill or legal-doctrinal curriculum is not guaranteed.

availableEvidence.description2: Introduces EU politics. Outlines actors, institutions and decision‑making rules; examines responses to crises; and employs various approaches to study EU politics and policy‑making.
availableEvidence.profile: Studies EU institutions, political actors, integration and policymaking, linking formal rules to current political issues. Students analyze representation, legitimacy, interests, agenda setting, decision-making and implementation. A substantial empirical project examines European Parliament committee amendments, connecting MEP ideology and possible interest-group influence to amendment activity. Students develop a project plan, code amendments, assess salience and trace legislative processes.
availableEvidence.topics: European integration; EU institutions and decision rules; EU legitimacy and democracy; Public opinion; Parties and European Parliament; Interest representation and lobbying; Agenda setting; EU legislation and implementation; MEP roles and committee behaviour; Political ideology and amendments; Policy salience
availableEvidence.methods: EU policy and legislative-document research; Process tracing; Systematic amendment coding; Ideology and amendment-activity analysis; Salience assessment; Comparative news-source analysis

courses.name: Econometrics
courses.rationale: The course description fully supports OLS/GLS/instrumental-variable estimation, causal/predictive questions, hypothesis tests and Stata/MonteCarlo work culminating in an empirical paper. These are policy-evaluation/economic evidence methods, not international trade or production-chain content.

availableEvidence.description2: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.

courses.name: Public Policy Analysis
courses.rationale: The available description directly supports policy-making phases across national/international arenas, a sugar case and policy memos. This is substantive public-policy analysis fully considered despite description-only evidence; environmental law or a particular pollution-policy case is not inferred.

availableEvidence.description2: Investigates public policy in the context of globalization. Uses a case study on sugar to examine policy‑making phases and alternative conceptualisations across national and international arenas. Students write policy memos.

courses.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
courses.rationale: Actual interviews, focus groups, document/visual approaches, coding/thematic interpretation and reflexive team research supply specific methods for stakeholder and policy inquiry. It is not a substitute for the full international environmental field-project course.

availableEvidence.description2: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
availableEvidence.profile: Develops qualitative inquiry from research design and preparation through data collection, management, analysis and dissemination. Students examine methodological foundations, ethics, positionality and reflexivity alongside interviews, focus groups, ethnography, documentary and visual approaches. Coding, thematic interpretation and NVivo support analysis. Research teams formulate a question, collect and analyze qualitative evidence, and report their methodological decisions, findings and limitations in staged assignments.
availableEvidence.topics: Qualitative knowledge and research design; Ethics, positionality and reflexivity; Mixed methods; Participatory research; Interview and focus-group approaches; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival sources; Visual and participatory media; Coding and thematic interpretation; Qualitative research dissemination
availableEvidence.methods: Qualitative research design; Interviews; Focus groups; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival analysis; Visual-data analysis; Participatory video and drawing; Transcription; Qualitative coding; Thematic analysis; NVivo-supported analysis; Reflexive methodological evaluation
